## Python Coder in UCloud

Today we will learn the fundamentals of Python in UCloud, where Python is already installed. This gives everyone a consistent setup and lets us focus on the language itself instead of troubleshooting software installation or technical setup.

Next week, when you use PsychoPy, you will install it on your laptop and work with the version of Python bundled with it. We start with plain Python first so you can build a solid foundation before adding the extra complexity of PsychoPy.

## How to open Python Coder in UCloud

1. Open [UCloud](https://cloud.sdu.dk/).

2. Go to your E26_LICS_Methods1 workspace using the drop-down menu in the top-left corner.

3. Open the Applications page by clicking the shopping bag icon in the right panel.

4. Search for "Coder" and click the application.

5. The Job Parameters page should open. Fill in the fields the same way you do for your RStudio jobs:

      a. Choose a meaningful job name
      b. Select the machine type (only one option is available)
      c. Click "Add Folder #1" and choose your cogsci_methods01_e26 folder
      d. Under "Initialization", select the ucloud_init_env_final.sh script
      e. Choose a reasonable number of hours

6. Click the green "Submit" button.

7. When the job is ready, click "Open Interface" at the top left.

## Install the Python language extension

Remember that we need to reinstall packages in UCloud every time we start a new job, because each job is assigned to a new remote computer. The same is true for Python: we need to install the Python language extension in the Coder application each time we start a new job. Here's how:

1. In the far-left panel, click the icon with four squares. This is the marketplace icon.

2. Type "Python" into the search bar. The Python extension should be at the top of the list (from ms-Python).

3. Click the Python extension, then click the Install button.


## Create your first Python code file

You can now create a new Python code file. Here's how:

1. In the far-left panel, find the icon that looks like three horizontal lines stacked on top of each other. Click it.

2. A pop-up menu will appear. Click *File > New File*.

3. A drop-down menu will appear asking for the file type. Type "Python" and you should see: *Create new file (python) Built-in*.

4. You will be prompted to choose where to save the file. For now, we will use:
   `/work/cogsci_methods01_e26/name_of_your_file.py`

You can choose any name for the file (it does not have to be "name_of_your_file.py"). The only rules are that you cannot use spaces and it must have a .py extension, because this tells the remote computer that it is a Python file when you reopen it later.

## "Hello world!": Run your first line of Python code

In your new code file, enter your first line of Python code:

```python
print("Hello world!")
```

::: {.predict-check data-answer="Hello world!"}
Your first prediction! Throughout these sessions, boxes like this ask you to guess what code will do *before* you run it. That's where the learning happens, and wrong guesses are very welcome and encouraged. After a few tries the box will offer to show you the answer, so you can never get stuck. So: what exactly will appear in the console when this line runs? Take a guess.

::: {.pc-explanation}
`Hello world!`. Note that there are no quotation marks. The quotes tell Python where the text starts and ends; they are not part of the text itself.
:::
:::

Now run the code by highlighting it and pressing Shift+Enter. You should see a dedicated terminal open below.

Terminal shows what you expected? Next: [Chapter 2 — Variables and types](02_variables.qmd).
